item.title: A Surprising Way to Get Unstuck In Your Life
item.description:
Growth Mindset

A Surprising Way to Get Unstuck In Your Life

Classic stories can help you overcome obstacles.

Posted June 24, 2026

Key points
  • Psychologists such as Maslow assert we all have an intrinsic need for personal growth.
  • This need explains why we like fictional characters who grow through adversity.
  • The emotional journeys of characters in classic literature show us how to grow in our own lives.

Feeling stuck?

Trapped in a job, a relationship, or an overweight or sickly body? Drifting through life without a direction or purpose? Yearning for something more, something vital in your life? If you’re like most people, the answer is ‘Yes.’ Realizing that is the easy part.

The harder part is knowing how to transform, heal, master, or whatever dimension of growth you seek. That’s why self-help books, which might as well all have the same title Three easy steps to becoming more than what you are, sell so well. They don’t so much sell insights about how to leave your old self behind as they sell raw, unrefined hope.

But there’s a more enjoyable way to learn how to grow: From stories.

The character arc

Working around Hollywood for over two decades, I learned that a script must have a satisfying character arc, where, for instance, the hero starts off wanting one thing, but through adversity, learns to sacrifice what they want to get what they truly need. For example, Rick Blaine, hero of Casablanca, starts off wanting Ilsa, but gives her up to embrace what he really needs: to recapture his idealism and pursuit of a better world. Rick became the person he could be, not the person he was.

That’s growth.

Hollywood demands stories driven by character transformations for a simple reason: audiences pay a lot to be inspired to become more than they are.

Why do we crave stories of personal growth so much?

Different branches of psychology have theorized why we strive to grow in our lives. Abraham Maslow famously asserted we intrinsically seek “self-actualization” as our ultimate goal in life after our other needs have been met [1]. Carl Rogers described an “actualizing tendency” that lives in all of us.[2] Robert White said that humans possess an “Effectance Motivation” that drives us to explore, practice, and master new skills [3]. Evolutionary psychology argues that drives such as actualization, found in every culture, are “evolved adaptations” that helped our ancestors thrive and reproduce, and were therefore passed down as heritable traits. [4]

These perspectives shed light on the psychology of growth, but there is a simpler explanation that Hollywood studios learned over a hundred years ago: if you give people hope, they will reward you. And the Hollywood message of hope goes like this: If (Rick Blain, Luke Skywalker, Ebenezer Scrooge) can change for the better, then so can I.

Stories that help you to grow the most

We are all natural imitation learners, so it should come as no surprise that a good way to learn and grow is by imitating someone else who faced and overcame challenges similar to yours. And not just in any story, but one that has stood the test of time.

The reason books like Tale of Two Cities (Sydney Carton overcomes self-loathing to embrace dignity and purpose), A Christmas Carol (Scrooge trades his lust for money for the warmth of fellowship), and Pinocchio (A wooden toy becomes a real boy by trading easy lies for hard honesty) became classics in the first place is precisely that their character arcs were so deeply relatable and satisfying.

Yes, you’ve read all these classics in high school, or earlier, but you probably didn’t read them explicitly looking for the character arcs. What wound did the protagonist start with? What obstacles did the character face—and fail to overcome— because they hadn’t learned what really matters in life? And most important, what made those characters realize they couldn’t heal the world without first healing themselves?

The classics are classics because almost everyone relates to the flaws in their characters and thus are inspired when the characters overcome themselves.

Here’s a free recipe for personal growth: find a protagonist in a classic story whose wound, failing, flaw, or compulsion maps onto yours, and pay close attention to what first gave that character insight about their ultimate need, then the motivation to sacrifice what they originally wanted to attain it. For instance, suppose you realize that you repeatedly self-sabotage relationships to avoid the risks of intimacy. You then ask an AI, “Which literary character grows by letting go of the fear of intimacy to find true love?”

An AI might respond, “In Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth Bennet begins guarded by pride, prejudice, and fear of vulnerability. By letting go of her defensive judgments and opening herself to genuine intimacy, she finds true love with Fitzwilliam Darcy.”

Rereading the novel to discover what prompted Elizabeth to grow, and how she did it, could be both inspirational and instructive. Yes, Elizabeth Bennet is a fictional character, but if her emotional journey weren’t real, Pride and Prejudice would be a forgotten relic, not a timeless classic. Classics are classics because they offer inspiring solutions to real problems.

Bottom line: The answers are gathering dust on your bookshelf, not in glittering bookstore self-help displays or snappy-looking online stores.

After you’ve re-read a few classics, you can start to write your own.

item.title: Recalibrating Friendships when Someone Changes
item.description:
Friends

Recalibrating Friendships when Someone Changes

Changing friendship dynamics can be difficult but necessary.

Posted June 24, 2026

Key points
  • Some friends resent when we make important life changes and may undermine or sabotage us.
  • People may grieve losing friends, even those who haven’t always had our best interests in mind.
  • Good friendships are founded on reciprocal goodwill and a shared commitment to becoming better people.
  • Good friendships contribute enormously to our happiness.

Friendships change over time because we humans are always changing. We both are and are not the same people we were one year ago, 10 years ago, or 50 years ago. Our friendships remind us of who we are and who we used to be. They also let us imagine who we could be.

When people change important parts of themselves, such as their moral commitments, political beliefs, religious convictions, or life-orienting activities, their friendships may change as well. They may need to recalibrate friendships and determine if, where, and how they fit into a person’s life. This can be very disorienting.

The “friends” who undermine and sabotage

Early in recovery from addiction, our friendship circles may undergo a seismic shift. If most of our friends had been our drinking or using buddies, being around them may elicit an avalanche of powerful and conflicting emotions on our part. The setup can also release some bad behavior by our friends, unfortunately.

Some of these friends may be unsupportive, while others actively sabotage efforts to be sober. Some will take your decision to reduce or stop as a judgment about them. They may even accuse you of making judgments about their use. Others will perceive your efforts at sobriety as a threat to them, especially if you have been using in the same way. You potentially disrupt their self-perception that they don’t have a problem.

Nothing will be able to convince these people that you are doing something for your own sake with no negative judgment about them. Some will actively make it harder for you not to use, or they will encourage you to use with them. As Epictetus (50-138 CE) counsels

Above all, keep a close watch on this—that you are never so tied to your former acquaintances and friends that you are pulled down to their level. If you don’t, you’ll be ruined... You must choose whether to be loved by these friends and remain the same person, or to become a better person at the cost of those friends...if you try to have it both ways you will neither make progress nor keep what you once had.

Manipulation and sabotage are quick routes to ruin. Anyone who uses those tools is not a friend.

Other friends may just toss you in the recycling bin and let you rattle around with all the empties. Your decision not to use makes you less fun or useful to them.

There is a pattern undergirding all these responses. Friends who care more about what they get out of a relationship rather than the other person are not good friends. They may not be friends at all because they make everything about them. There is no reciprocal goodwill, which is a minimal requirement for friendship.

We are not always prepared to grieve friendships and face the disorientation that follows from losing them. This is especially true with long-term friends; so much of our histories are woven together. We may not even know who we are without them.

People who have fewer friendships in their lives may also find these losses disorienting or even intolerable. We may tell ourselves, If I leave this friendship, I will be totally alone. I don’t know how to make friends. The fear of loneliness may be the reason people stay in friendships that are so asymmetrical, unsatisfying, and risky.

Cultivating friends who help us become better people

There are positive shifts in our friendships early in recovery as well. We may discover that some of the people who had put some distance between us never fully went away. We may realize that some of the friends we had pruned from our lives are open to reconnecting when they see that we are trying to live very differently. In both cases, we need to practice patience.

People can have goodwill towards you but not throw their arms wide open. Friendships are based on trust, and our addictions may have corroded a lot of it. Friendships require work and maintenance.

Friendships, according to Aristotle (384-322 BCE), are activities that take time and effort to cultivate and then tend. The best kind of friendship is when the two people have the same sort of moral character and commitment to becoming better people. We become better people, according to Aristotle, in the presence of our friends. They provide us with opportunities to develop our moral character by cultivating moral virtues such as trust, generosity, courage, humility, honesty, and self-respect.

The right sort of friend always has our best interests front and center; there are no hidden agendas. They want what is best for us for our own sake and not for any benefit they may derive. They have a commitment to our moral growth, which manifests itself in several ways. Good friends:

  • Act as moral mirrors to us. They reflect our actions and our character back to us. We may see ourselves most clearly in how our friends see us.
  • Encourage us to pursue what makes us better people and avoid what would harm our character.
  • Offer us assistance when we stumble and help us figure out why that happened.
  • Teach us how to love ourselves. For Aristotle, self-love and the love for a friend are deeply and fundamentally connected. They are models for each other. What we should love in our friend is their moral character, which is what we should love about ourselves.
  • Are our second selves. When we hurt a friend, we hurt ourselves. And when we hurt ourselves, we hurt our friends.

Friendships, for Aristotle, are necessary for the best possible life. In recovery, we can forge new friendships and revisit older ones. One of the greatest gifts in recovery is friendship. As Seneca (4 BCE-65 CE) wisely notes, “No good thing is pleasant to possess, without friends to share it.”

item.title: 3 Strategies to Make a Breakup Easier
item.description:
Relationships

3 Strategies to Make a Breakup Easier

How to break up with someone while avoiding ghosting, arguing, or hurt feelings.

Posted June 24, 2026

Key points
  • Due to emotional and interpersonal concerns, it can be difficult to end a relationship and break up.
  • Those concerns can cause people to suffer in silence, or ghost their partner, rather than talking it out.
  • Strategies to discuss the breakup indirectly, however, can ease tension and make the conversation easier.

I’m concluding this series on navigating difficult conversations in dating and relationships with one of the most challenging discussions—breaking up with someone. It is hard enough to face rejection and ask someone out in the first place. It is even more difficult to talk about intensifying a relationship and asking for greater commitment. But ending a relationship or marriage, especially after all that investment and commitment, is difficult and anxiety-provoking for sure.

Fortunately, however, many of the indirect “face-saving strategies” used in those other conversations are helpful when breaking up or divorcing someone, too. Kunkel, Wilson, Olufowote, and Robson (2003) identified specific strategies that individuals use to disengage from romantic relationships while reducing awkwardness, embarrassment, and hurt feelings. If you don’t like the usual choices of staying or ghosting, then read on—and learn some better options.

Concerns Before Breaking Up

To better understand those options, however, we first need to learn what makes ending a relationship so awkward. What basic concerns are we wrestling with in that conversation? Aiding us in that understanding, Kunkel and associates (2003) note six main concerns that individuals consider before ending a relationship:

  • Why do I want to break up with my partner right now?
  • Are they unable to break up with me for some reason (no other place to live)?
  • Do I have the right to decide to end the relationship by myself?
  • Why do I need to be the one to end the relationship (don’t they already know it is failing)?
  • Do they seem like they are willing to break up?
  • Do I really want to end the relationship (and lose out on any remaining benefits)?

Studying these concerns further, Kunkel and team (2003) found that individuals considering breaking up with a partner are often worried that “the partner will feel pressured to comply, they could later regret having ended the relationship, the [partner] may appear inadequate, and they themselves may appear insensitive” (p.402-403). Of particular concern to participants was the effect the breakup might have on other relationships (children, family, friends, and other potential partners). Participants were also concerned about not being too forward and threatening their partner’s autonomy.

Despite those concerns, 100 percent of participants surveyed said that they would speak with a partner about ending a relationship if it was warranted. Furthermore, even if their partner initially refused to have the discussion, 86 percent said they would continue in their efforts to end the relationship in the future. To persist in those efforts, however, many chose a less risky and anxiety-provoking option—discussing things indirectly.

Indirect Breakup Strategies

More exploration by Kunkel and associates (2003) found that some participants shared indirect strategies to save face and reduce anxiety while discussing a breakup with a partner. Those indirect strategies were categorized into three levels:
(1) very indirect, with only mild hints about breaking up
(2) somewhat indirect, with strong hints about breaking up
(3) somewhat direct with preliminary conversation leading to a more direct statement ending the relationship. Beyond that, each strategy had a specific approach, as discussed below:

Participants with a very indirect strategy began by providing mild hints and sharing general feelings about the relationship. They also listened and paid attention to their partner’s reactions and opinions, too. This approach avoided blaming their partner and helped everyone feel understood, which follows the general strategy to calm arguments I suggest in my book Attraction Psychology (Nicholson, 2022). Essentially, this is a first step to gently identify annoying problems that are reducing relationship satisfaction—and decide whether they can be fixed and forgiven. Sometimes, however, a partner is resistant to mild hints, or the relationship is beyond repair, and additional strategies are required.

Thus, participants with a somewhat indirect strategy moved on to providing stronger hints, sharing their negative feelings about the relationship, and making a request to step back from the relationship to figure things out. For example, Kunkel and associates (2003) note that participants suggested telling a partner that “things didn’t feel the same anymore,” that they “didn’t know what they wanted,” and they “needed some time apart to think” (p. 399). This approach offers two benefits. On one hand, it gives the partner some information about what is going on, avoiding the anxious and uncertain reactions that can come from ghosting. On the other hand, if circumstances do change, it also provides a path for reconciliation. Nevertheless, some partners can still feel a bit blindsided and may require additional information to understand what exactly is changing and why.

As a result, participants with a somewhat direct strategy may follow up with a specific request to end or redefine the relationship after completing the first two strategies above. Participants using this strategy suggested inquiring about their partner’s perceptions (“Is it just me, or do you think things between us have changed too?”). Kunkel and associates (2003) then report participants followed up with general reasons why they wanted the relationship to end (“I feel like the only reason we’re still in this relationship is that we’ve been together so long.”) and a specific request to take a break or breakup entirely (“I think we need to split up before things get any worse.”). This approach shows empathy, avoids blame, and allows for the possibility of a mutually beneficial path forward, which are essential parts of breaking up compassionately. Therefore, it offers the best chance at stepping back or ending a relationship with the least amount of anxiety, argument, and hurt feelings possible.

item.title: Mental Illness Caused by ‘Gene Parasites’
item.description:
Genetics

Mental Illness Caused by ‘Gene Parasites’

Can mental illness be driven by ancient viral infection and corrupt our DNA?

Posted June 24, 2026

Key points
  • Ancient viral DNA, or ERVs, make up 8% of the human genome and disrupt gene regulation.
  • Viral DNA inserted into the genome of our ancestors can drive many mental illnesses for generations.
  • ERVs are linked to neurological and psychiatric disorders like autism, schizophrenia, and ALS.
Source: Kai Stachowiak, CCO public domain

Could a viral infection you experience today cause mental health disorders for generations of your descendants? Absolutely. Many psychological disorders are driven by a viral infection in prehistoric times that disrupted DNA and has been passed down through generations.

Viruses survive as genetic parasites because they must infect healthy cells to reproduce. Viruses hijack the host’s genetic operation because they do not have the cellular machinery to make their own proteins.

Dreadful cancers and other illnesses can be caused by viral infection, but less widely appreciated is that DNA that was inserted into the genome of our ancient human ancestors from viral infection can cause psychological and neurological disorders through generations.

Briefly, here is the diabolical way viruses hack into our genes.

Retroviruses, like HIV, infect cells and inject their genetic material, RNA, into the host cell. The viral RNA is converted to DNA and inserted into the infected cell’s genome like malicious software code infecting a computer program. When the cell reads that foreign DNA code, it unwittingly generates viral proteins and produces swarms of the virus.

This viral genetic sabotage is a reversal of the normal operation that cells use to make a specific protein needed for cell structure and function. Normally, the instructions to make a particular protein are coded in a stretch of DNA, which is a durable genetic blueprint locked inside the cell’s nucleus.

A copy of the DNA instructions for a gene is made by a string of RNA that leaves the nucleus to deliver the information to the cell’s machinery that synthesizes the protein specified. Like a Post-It note, RNA is a short-lived molecule meant to jot down information temporarily. The RNA is quickly discarded so that the cell does not get bogged down by outdated information, while the master blueprint is preserved inside the cell nucleus. By converting its viral RNA into DNA, the infecting virus reverse-engineers the normal process. That, however, can cause long-lasting genetic haywire.

Sometimes, DNA made from viral RNA, or snippets of it, can become permanently embedded in the host’s DNA and inherited for generations by the descendants. These bits of foreign DNA may no longer produce viruses, but they can put a monkey wrench into the cellular works.

The viral DNA is often inserted into long stretches of DNA that do not code for genes, but are instead regions of DNA, called introns, that control the switching synthesis of a gene on or off. Only 2 percent of the human genome is genes, and the rest of the DNA controls when a gene is produced. Fouling up the intricate control of gene production can wreak havoc on a cell. These ancient bits of viral DNA stuck inside our genome are known as endogenous retroviruses (ERVs), and they comprise 8 percent of human DNA.

Multiple sclerosis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s disorder, and other neurological and cognitive disorders are known to be triggered by ERVs. A growing number of studies link these retroviral DNA elements with neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders.

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) patients have significantly higher levels of a particular ERV (HERV-H), compared to healthy children. Similar findings have been found for other ERVs, and some other ERVs (HERV-W) are unusually scarce in children with ASD.

Abnormal ERVs have also been identified in schizophrenia, a major psychiatric disorder affecting up to 1 percent of the world’s population. Some 29 percent of people with recent-onset schizophrenic disorder have snippets of HERV-W in their cerebrospinal fluid. Abnormal ERV appearance has also been identified in people with bipolar depression. Postmortem analysis of the brains of people with schizophrenia and several other mental disorders shows abnormal traces of ancient viral genes (ERVs) in brain regions known to be disrupted in the psychiatric disorder.

This new information expands understanding of the biological basis of mental illnesses, but it is important to recognize that our fate is not necessarily cast at birth by our genes. As in most things in biology, health and illness result from interactions between genes and the environment. Stress, environmental toxins, and inflammation can activate ERVs.

It is startling to realize that what we believe to be the most complicated structure in the known universe, the human brain, can be undermined by the most primitive form of life—a virus that has parasitized human DNA over eons.
